extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of philosophy; aspiring philosophers, critics, and thoughtful readers of philosophical/poetic prose
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for how to read, judge, and decide whether to engage with philosophical treatises (including poetic/philosophical prose); who will benefit and what mental dispositions/methods are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presume your ignorance of the writer's understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: “Until you understand a writer’s ignorance, presume yourself ignorant of his understanding.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reading difficult or obscure philosophical writing, try first to grasp the limits or errors in the author's knowledge (their 'ignorance') before assuming you understand their intellectual grasp. Examples in the text: re-reading Plato's TIMAEUS where parts remain unintelligible—one should avoid dismissing as jargon without searching for causes of the apparent inconsistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain supernatural or ecstatic claims by natural causes before accusing dishonesty
rubrics_metrics.description: In encountering accounts of dreams and supernatural experiences, seek bodily or psychological causes and explain 'all the strange incidents... without suspecting him of any intentional falsehood.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a writer reports visionary or fanatical experiences, attempt to interpret them in terms of known bodily/mental laws rather than immediately attributing mendacity; follow traces as calmly as tracking a fog-bound traveller.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read whole connectedly or not at all
rubrics_metrics.description: The reader is asked 'either pass over the following chapter altogether, or read the whole connectedly.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not excerpt delicate philosophical material: isolated passages can produce a 'skeleton' or monstrous impression; for subtle arguments or nuanced forms, read the entire connected argument to avoid distortion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not require an unprejudiced mind as a precondition (but be aware of prejudice limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: The author will not demand that the reader be wholly free of prejudices or prior systems, acknowledging that asking absolute impartiality is impractical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While an open mind is desirable, the writer concedes one cannot reasonably expect readers to erase all prior opinions; instead, temper expectations and suggest readiness rather than impossible neutrality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a readiness criterion to decide if the work is for you
rubrics_metrics.description: If a man receives as fundamental facts the general notions of matter, spirit, soul, body, action, passiveness, time, space, cause and effect, consciousness, perception, memory and habit as indemonstrable and final, 'for him the chapter was not written.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before investing time and temper in this treatise, test whether you hold those listed concepts as unexamined, ultimate principles; if so, you will likely gain little and should refrain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize that philosophy is not for all; require the philosophic organ
rubrics_metrics.description: It is 'neither possible nor necessary for all men, nor for many, to be philosophers'—there is an 'artificial' philosophic consciousness or organ that some possess and others lack.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept that some readers will find philosophical works obscure not from authorial failure but from lack of inner sense/intuitive faculty; don't judge such opacity solely as the writer's fault.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare by cultivating receptive patience for intuitive knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: On the highest and intuitive knowledge: 'we ought not to pursue it with a view of detecting its secret source, but to watch in quiet till it suddenly shines upon us; preparing ourselves for the blessed spectacle as the eye waits patiently for the rising sun.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acquire readiness by quiet attention and moral/practical preparation rather than attempting forceful analytic extraction; philosophical imagination may 'suddenly' appear to the prepared mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept postulates (primary intuitions) in philosophy as in mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophy, like geometry, must commence from a primary intuition or postulate (the 'original construction'); the mathematician begins with an intuition/point or line that is postulated rather than demonstrated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophical argument may legitimately begin from postulated first-acts of inner sense; introduction of such postulates should be treated as necessary when seeking evidence in philosophy, analogous to geometry's axioms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophy's foundational postulate: Know thyself (coincidence of subject and object)
rubrics_metrics.description: The postulate and the test of philosophic capacity is 'KNOW THYSELF!' — all knowledge rests on coincidence of object with subject; philosophy's primary ground is both practical and speculative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophical inquiry must ground itself in self-intuition—simultaneously practical and speculative—because truth depends on the coincidence of thought and thing; cultivate self-knowledge as philosophical method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain methodological purity between natural and transcendental philosophy
rubrics_metrics.description: In pursuing sciences, adhere to each science's principles and 'exclude those which appertain to the opposite science'—natural philosophers should avoid subjective suppositions; transcendental philosophers should avoid empirical pictures substituted for immediate objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the methods and assumptions of natural (objective) philosophy and transcendental (subjective/intelligential) philosophy distinct to avoid category errors; use 'absolute and scientific scepticism' to purify the mind for proper inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat the belief in 'things without us' as a prejudice to be interrogated
rubrics_metrics.description: The presumption 'THAT THERE EXIST THINGS WITHOUT US' is an innate prejudice—immediate, irresistible, but not demonstrable—and the transcendental philosopher should treat it as such and seek to show its identity with self-consciousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than accepting external realism by habit, examine how belief in external things may be unconsciously involved in, or identical with, immediate self-consciousness; this interrogation is central to transcendental method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thesis I — Truth must correspond to being
rubrics_metrics.description: THESIS I: 'Truth is correlative to being. Knowledge without a correspondent reality is no knowledge; if we know, there must be somewhat known by us.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a principle to judge claims: require that alleged knowledge has a corresponding reality; knowledge is an active relation to being.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thesis II — Distinguish immediate and mediate truth
rubrics_metrics.description: THESIS II: 'All truth is either mediate... or immediate and original. The latter is absolute, and its formula A. A.; the former is of dependent or conditional certainty, and represented in the formula B. A.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify propositions as immediate (self-evident, absolute) or mediate (derived and conditionally certain); this distinction guides which claims require further demonstration versus which are foundational.
